<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:existence}
	Let $d\ge1$, $m>0$, $\omega>0$ and $2<p<2^{*}=\frac{2d}{d-1}$
	(with $2^{*}=\infty$ if $d=1$). Then \eqref{eq:main} admits a ground state
	$Q\in H^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ that is positive, radial and radially
	nonincreasing. Equivalently, after the scaling normalization $\omega=1$, the sharp
	constant in the pseudo-relativistic Weinstein--Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:wgn}
		\|u\|_{p}\;\le\;C_{m,p}\,
		\big\langle\sqrt{-\Delta+m^{2}}\,u,u\big\rangle^{\theta/2}\,
		\|u\|_{2}^{\,1-\theta},
		\qquad
		\theta:=d\Big(\tfrac12-\tfrac1p\Big)\in(0,1),
	\end{equation}
	is attained, and every optimizer equals $Q$ up to a positive multiple and a dilation.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Let $d\ge1$, $m>0$, $\omega>0$ and $2<p<2^{*}$. Then \eqref{eq:main} has a unique
positive radial variational ground state.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:Jm-gauss}
	Let $m>0$, 
	\[
	\nu_m(\tau):=\frac{m}{\sqrt{4\pi}}\,\tau^{-3/2}e^{-m^2\tau}
	\qquad
	g_\tau(r):=(4\pi\tau)^{-d/2}e^{-r^2/(4\tau)},
	\qquad
	d\mu_m:=\nu_m\,d\tau\ge0 .
	\]
	Then
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Jm-gauss}
		J_m(\left|z\right|)=\int_0^\infty g_\tau(\left|z\right|)\,d\mu_m(\tau),
	\end{equation}
	and for each $\tau>0$, $g_\tau$ is radial, strictly decreasing, $\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}g_\tau=1$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Throughout we use the convention
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:convention}
		\hat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(z)e^{-iz\cdot\xi}\,dx z,
		\qquad
		\mathcal F^{-1}[f](z)=(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(\xi)e^{iz\cdot\xi}\,d\xi ,
	\end{equation}
	for which Plancherel's theorem reads
	$\left\langle f,g\right\rangle=(2\pi)^{-d}\left\langle \hat f,\hat g\right\rangle$, and \eqref{eq:Am-form} takes the form
	$\left\langle A_{m} u,u\right\rangle=(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}\,\left|\hat u(\xi)\right|^2\,d\xi$.
	
	\emph{Step 1.} For $\psi_m(\lambda):=\sqrt{\lambda+m^2}-m$, we have
	\[
	\psi_m(0)=0,\qquad
	\psi_m'(\lambda)=\tfrac12(\lambda+m^2)^{-1/2}>0,\qquad
	\psi_m''(\lambda)=-\tfrac14(\lambda+m^2)^{-3/2}<0,
	\]
	\[
	(-1)^{n-1}\psi_m^{(n)}\ge0\ (n\ge1),
	\quad \text{and} \quad
	\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\frac{\psi_m(\lambda)}{\lambda}=0 .
	\]
	Hence $\psi_m$ is a complete Bernstein function with vanishing killing and drift terms. From \cite[Ch.~5]{SSV}, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:bernstein}
		\sqrt{\lambda+m^2}-m=\int_0^\infty\big(1-e^{-\tau\lambda}\big)\,\nu_m(\tau)\,d\tau,
		\qquad\lambda\ge0 .
	\end{equation}
	Setting $\lambda=\left|\xi\right|^2$, we see that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:symbol-decomp}
		\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}-m=\int_0^\infty\big(1-e^{-\tau\left|\xi\right|^2}\big)\,\nu_m(\tau)\,d\tau .
	\end{equation}
	
	\emph{Step 2.} It follows from \eqref{eq:convention} that
	\[
	\mathcal F^{-1}\big[e^{-\tau\left|\xi\right|^2}\big](z)
	=(2\pi)^{-d}\prod_{j=1}^{d}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-\tau\xi_j^2+iz_j\xi_j}\,d\xi_j
	=(2\pi)^{-d}\Big(\tfrac{\pi}{\tau}\Big)^{d/2}e^{-\left|z\right|^2/(4\tau)}
	=g_\tau(\left|z\right|),
	\]
	where each factor is computed by completing the square,
	$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-\tau\xi_j^2+iz_j\xi_j}d\xi_j
	=e^{-z_j^2/(4\tau)}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-\tau(\xi_j-iz_j/(2\tau))^2}d\xi_j
	=\sqrt{\pi/\tau}\,e^{-z_j^2/(4\tau)}.$$
	Applying $\mathcal F$ to both sides and evaluating at $\xi=0$, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:gauss-fourier}
		\widehat{g_\tau}(\xi)=e^{-\tau\left|\xi\right|^2}
		\quad \text{and} \quad
		\widehat{g_\tau}(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}g_\tau=1 ,
	\end{equation}
	the last identity because $\hat k(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}k(z)e^{-iz\cdot0}\,dx z=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}k$ for any
	$k\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^{d})$.
	
	\emph{Step 3.} Let $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ be real and let $k\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ be symmetric.
	Expanding $\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2=\left|u(x)\right|^2+\left|u(y)\right|^2-2u(x)u(y)$ and using the
	translation invariance, we obtain
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:khat0}
		\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}k(x-y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}k(z)\,dx z=\hat k(0),
	\end{equation}
	Fubini's thorem gives, for the first two terms,
	\[
	\tfrac12\iint\big(\left|u(x)\right|^2+\left|u(y)\right|^2\big)k(x-y)\,dx\,dy=\hat k(0)\,\left\|u\right\|_2^2 ,
	\]
	while the cross term is a convolution, so that by $\widehat{k*u}=\hat k\,\hat u$ and
	Plancherel's theorem,
	\[
	-\iint u(x)k(x-y)u(y)\,dx\,dy=-\left\langle k*u,u\right\rangle
	=-(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\hat k(\xi)\left|\hat u(\xi)\right|^2\,d\xi .
	\]
	Since $\left\|u\right\|_2^2=(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left|\hat u\right|^2\,d\xi$, adding the two displays yields
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:diff-symbol}
		\tfrac12\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2 k(x-y)\,dx\,dy
		=(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big(\hat k(0)-\hat k(\xi)\big)\left|\hat u(\xi)\right|^2\,d\xi .
	\end{equation}
	By \eqref{eq:gauss-fourier}, \eqref{eq:diff-symbol} with $k=g_\tau$ gives
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:gauss-form}
		\tfrac12\iint\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2 g_\tau(\left|x-y\right|)\,dx\,dy
		=(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big(1-e^{-\tau\left|\xi\right|^2}\big)\left|\hat u(\xi)\right|^2\,d\xi .
	\end{equation}
	Integrating \eqref{eq:gauss-form} in $\tau$ against $\nu_m\ge0$, using \eqref{eq:symbol-decomp},  Tonelli's theorem,
	Plancherel's theorem and \eqref{eq:Am-form}, then, we obtain
	\begin{align}
		\tfrac12\iint\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2\Big(\int_0^\infty g_\tau(\left|x-y\right|)\,\nu_m(\tau)\,d\tau\Big)\,dx\,dy
		&=(2\pi)^{-d}\!\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big(1-e^{-\tau\left|\xi\right|^2}\big)\left|\hat u\right|^2\nu_m(\tau)\,d\xi\,d\tau
		\notag\\
		&=(2\pi)^{-d}\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big(\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}-m\big)\left|\hat u(\xi)\right|^2\,d\xi
		\notag\\
		&=\left\langle (A_{m}-m)u,u\right\rangle \notag\\
		&=\tfrac12\iint\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2 J_m(\left|x-y\right|)\,dx\,dy .
		\label{eq:two-forms}
	\end{align}
	As \eqref{eq:two-forms} holds for all $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and both kernels are radial,
	they agree a.e., which is \eqref{eq:Jm-gauss}.
	
	\emph{Step 4.} $g_\tau(z)=(4\pi\tau)^{-d/2}e^{-\left|z\right|^2/(4\tau)}$ depends on $z$ only
	through $\left|z\right|$, is strictly decreasing in $\left|z\right|$, and $\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}g_\tau=1$ by
	\eqref{eq:gauss-fourier}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:green}
	Let $G_{m}$ denote the kernel of $(A_{m}+1)^{-1}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, i.e.\ the radial positive solution
	of $(A_{m}+1)G_{m}=\delta_{0}$. Then $G_{m}>0$, $G_{m}$ is radially strictly decreasing,
	$G_{m}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$, and there are constants $C_{d,m}\ge1$, $R_0\ge1$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:green}
		C_{d,m}^{-1}\,\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|}
		\;\le\;G_{m}(x)\;\le\;
		C_{d,m}\,\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|},
		\qquad \left|x\right|\ge R_0 .
	\end{equation}
	Near the origin, $G_{m}(x)\simeq\left|x\right|^{-(d-1)}$ for $d\ge2$ and
	$G_{m}(x)\simeq\log\tfrac1{\left|x\right|}$ for $d=1$. Moreover, for every $m'<m$, there holds that 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:green-upper}
		G_{m}(x)\le C\,e^{-m'\left|x\right|},\qquad \left|x\right|\ge1.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
\emph{Subordination: positivity, strict monotonicity, integrability.}
	By Proposition~\ref{prop:Jm-gauss}, $\psi_m(\lambda)=\sqrt{\lambda+m^2}-m$ is a complete
	Bernstein function, so $A_{m}-m$ is subordinate to $-\Delta$ and the semigroup $e^{-tA_{m}}$
	has kernel
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:subord}
		p_{t}^{m}(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-\left|x\right|^{2}/(4\tau)}}{(4\pi\tau)^{d/2}}\,
		\eta_{t}^{m}(\tau)\,d\tau ,
		\qquad \eta_{t}^{m}>0\ \text{ on }(0,\infty),
	\end{equation}
	where $\eta_t^m$ is the transition density of the relativistic $\tfrac12$-stable
	subordinator \cite[Ch.~5, Ch.~13]{SSV}. Each Gaussian in \eqref{eq:subord} is positive and
	strictly decreasing in $\left|x\right|$, and $\eta_t^m>0$. Thus, $p_t^m>0$ and $p_t^m$ is strictly
	decreasing in $\left|x\right|$. Writing the resolvent as the Laplace transform of the semigroup,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:resolvent-laplace}
		G_{m}(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}\,p_{t}^{m}(x)\,dt ,
	\end{equation}
	these properties are inherited by $G_{m}$: $G_{m}>0$ and $G_{m}$ is radially strictly
	decreasing. Since $G_{m}\ge0$,
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}G_{m}=\widehat{G_{m}}(0)=\big(\sqrt{0+m^{2}}+1\big)^{-1}=(m+1)^{-1}<\infty ,
	\]
	then $G_{m}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$.
	
	\emph{Decay.} The two-sided bound \eqref{eq:green} is the exponential-decay regime for the
	resolvent kernel $\int_0^\infty e^{-t}p_t^m(x)\,dt$ of a relativistic operator,
	established by Carmona--Masters--Simon \cite{CMS}; see also Kaleta--Schilling--Sztonyk
	\cite{KSS} for sharp two-sided estimates of resolvent kernels of L\'evy operators covering
	this case. The bound \eqref{eq:green-upper} follows from the upper bound in
	\eqref{eq:green} by absorbing the algebraic prefactor into $e^{-(m-m')\left|x\right|}$. The
	behaviour near the origin follows from \eqref{eq:Jm-asy}: for small $\left|x\right|$ both the mass
	and the ``$+1$'' are lower-order perturbations, so $G_{m}$ inherits the leading singularity
	of the kernel of $(-\Delta)^{-1/2}$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:green}
	Only the exponential rate $m$ and the algebraic prefactor $\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}$ in
	\eqref{eq:green} are used below; no exact constant is needed. Accordingly all decay
	statements in this paper are formulated as two-sided bounds rather than exact asymptotics.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:convolution}
	Let $H,F\ge0$ be radial, $H,F\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and $F\not\equiv0$. Assume  
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:conv-hyp}
		c_H^{-1}\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|}\le H(x)\le c_H\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|},
		\ \ \left|x\right|\ge R_0
		\quad \text{and} \quad
		F(x)\le c_F\,e^{-m''\left|x\right|},\ \ x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},
	\end{equation}
	for some	$c_H,c_F\ge1$, $R_0\ge1$, $m''>m$.
	Then there are $C\ge1$, $R_1\ge R_0$ with
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:conv-concl}
		C^{-1}\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|}\le(H*F)(x)\le C\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|},
		\qquad \left|x\right|\ge R_1 .
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We write $(H*F)(x)=I_1(x)+I_2(x)$, where
	\[
	I_1(x):=\int_{\{\left|x-y\right|>\left|x\right|/2\}}H(x-y)F(y)\,dy,
	\qquad
	I_2(x):=\int_{\{\left|x-y\right|\le\left|x\right|/2\}}H(x-y)F(y)\,dy,
	\]
	and let $\left|x\right|\ge2R_0$.
	
On $\{\left|x-y\right|>\left|x\right|/2\}$ we have $\left|x-y\right|>\left|x\right|/2\ge R_0$,
	so \eqref{eq:conv-hyp} applies and, together with $\left|x-y\right|\ge\left|x\right|-\left|y\right|$,
	\[
	H(x-y)\le c_H\left|x-y\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x-y\right|}
	\le c_H2^{\frac{d+1}{2}}\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|}e^{m\left|y\right|}.
	\]
	Since $F(y)e^{m\left|y\right|}\le c_Fe^{-(m''-m)\left|y\right|}\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^{d})$,
	\[
	I_1(x)\le c_H2^{\frac{d+1}{2}}\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}F(y)e^{m\left|y\right|}\,dy .
	\]
	
 Fix $\rho\ge1$ with $\int_{\left|y\right|\le\rho}F>0$. For
	$\left|x\right|\ge\max(4R_0,4\rho)$ and $\left|y\right|\le\rho$ we have
	$\left|x\right|/2\le\left|x\right|-\rho\le\left|x-y\right|\le\left|x\right|+\rho\le2\left|x\right|$, so $\{\left|y\right|\le\rho\}$ is
	contained in the domain of $I_1$ and
	\[
	H(x-y)\ge c_H^{-1}\left|x-y\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x-y\right|}
	\ge c_H^{-1}2^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\rho}\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|},
	\]
	whence
	$I_1(x)\ge c_H^{-1}2^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\rho}\big(\int_{\left|y\right|\le\rho}F\big)
	\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|}$.
	
 On $\{\left|x-y\right|\le\left|x\right|/2\}$ we have
	$\left|y\right|\ge\left|x\right|-\left|x-y\right|\ge\left|x\right|/2$, so $F(y)\le c_Fe^{-m''\left|y\right|}\le c_Fe^{-m''\left|x\right|/2}$,
	and since $H\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^{d})$,
	\[
	I_2(x)\le c_F\,e^{-m''\left|x\right|/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}H
	=c_F\left\|H\right\|_{L^1}\,e^{-m''\left|x\right|/2}.
	\]
Using $e^{-m''\left|y\right|}=e^{-m\left|y\right|}e^{-(m''-m)\left|y\right|}$ and 
	$\left|y\right|\ge\left|x\right|/2$ together with $\left|x-y\right|\le\left|x\right|/2$, we get
	$\left|x-y\right|+\left|y\right|\ge\left|x\right|$, hence
	\[
	I_2(x)\le c_F\,e^{-m\left|x\right|}e^{-\frac{m''-m}{2}\left|x\right|}\left\|H\right\|_{L^1}
	=o\big(\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|}\big)
	\]
	as $\left|x\right|\to\infty$, since $m''>m$. Combining the three estimates yields
	\eqref{eq:conv-concl}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
By the scaling,  it suffices to produce a minimizer
	for $m$ fixed and $\omega=1$. The case of general $\omega$ follows by the transformation
	$P(x)=\omega^{-1/(p-2)}Q(\omega^{-1}x)$. We construct the ground state as a minimizer of a
	constrained variational problem, then upgrade it to a positive radial nonincreasing
	solution of \eqref{eq:norm}.
	
	\medskip
\emph{Step 1.}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Sinf}
	S:=\inf\Big\{\,B(u):\ u\inH^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\ \left\|u\right\|_p=1\,\Big\},
	\qquad B(u):=\left\langle A_{m} u,u\right\rangle+\left\|u\right\|_2^2 .
\end{equation}
By the  Fourier transform, with $\displaystyle\left\|u\right\|_{H^{1/2}}^2=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}\left|\hat u\right|^2$, we have
\[
B(u)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big(\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}+1\big)\,\left|\hat u(\xi)\right|^2\,d\xi .
\]
We claim the two weights $w(\xi):=\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}+1$ and $(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}$ are
pointwise comparable, with constants depending only on $m$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weight}
	\tfrac{1}{2}\,(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}\;\le\;w(\xi)\;\le\;(m+2)\,(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2},
	\qquad \xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d} .
\end{equation}

If $\left|\xi\right|\ge1$, then
$w(\xi)\ge\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2}=\left|\xi\right|$.  Since $1\le\left|\xi\right|^2$, we have
\[
(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}\le(2\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}=\sqrt2\,\left|\xi\right|\le2\left|\xi\right| ,
\]
whence $w(\xi)\ge\left|\xi\right|\ge\tfrac12(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}$. 

If $\left|\xi\right|\le1$, then
$w(\xi)\ge1$, while
$(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}\le\sqrt2\le2$. Thus, we have 
$w(\xi)\ge1\ge\tfrac12(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}$.
Using $\sqrt{a+b}\le\sqrt a+\sqrt b$, we have 
\[
w(\xi)=\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}+1\le\left|\xi\right|+m+1.
\]
Combing $\left|\xi\right|\le(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}$ with   $1\le(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}$, it follows that
\[
w(\xi)\le(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}+(m+1)(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2}=(m+2)(1+\left|\xi\right|^2)^{1/2} .
\]

Multiplying \eqref{eq:weight} by $\left|\hat u(\xi)\right|^2\ge0$ and integrating yields the norm
equivalence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:B-equiv}
	\tfrac12\,\left\|u\right\|_{H^{1/2}}^2\;\le\;B(u)\;\le\;(m+2)\,\left\|u\right\|_{H^{1/2}}^2 ,
	\qquad u\inH^{1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).
\end{equation}
By the Sobolev embedding $H^{1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\hookrightarrow L^p(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ for $2\le p<2^*$ and \eqref{eq:B-equiv},
\[
\left\|u\right\|_p\le C\left\|u\right\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\sqrt2\,B(u)^{1/2}=:C'B(u)^{1/2}.
\]
Restricting to the constraint $\left\|u\right\|_p=1$ gives $1\le C'B(u)^{1/2}$, i.e.\
$B(u)\ge(C')^{-2}$. Taking  the infimum, we obtain $S\ge(C')^{-2}>0$. Hence $S>0$ and any minimizing
sequence $(u_n)\subsetH^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ (i.e.\ $\left\|u_n\right\|_p=1$, $B(u_n)\to S$) satisfies
$\left\|u_n\right\|_{H^{1/2}}^2\le2B(u_n)\le C''$ by \eqref{eq:B-equiv}, so $(u_n)$ is bounded in
$H^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$.
	
	\medskip
	\emph{Step 2.}
Since the radial embedding $	H^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\hookrightarrow\hookrightarrow L^p(\mathbb{R}^{d})$
	is compact (Lions' radial compactness for $H^{1/2}$; see \cite[Prop.~3.5]{Secchi} for the
	Bessel formulation, or Sickel--Skrzypczak for the general fractional radial embedding).
	By Step~1, $(u_n)$ is bounded in $H^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}$, passing to a subsequence, we have 
	\[
	u_n\rightharpoonup Q\ \text{ in }H^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\qquad u_n\to Q\ \text{ in }L^p(\mathbb{R}^{d}).
	\]
	Strong $L^p$-convergence gives $\left\|Q\right\|_p=\lim_n\left\|u_n\right\|_p=1$, so $Q\not\equiv0$ and $Q$
	is admissible for \eqref{eq:Sinf}. The functional $B$ is a nonnegative energy functional, then,
by weakly lower semicontinuous,  we  have 
	\[
	B(Q)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}B(u_n)=S .
	\]
	Since $Q$ is admissible, $B(Q)\ge S$. Therefore $B(Q)=S$ and $Q$ attains the infimum.
	
	\medskip
\emph{Step 3.}
We show the minimizer may be taken nonnegative, radial and radially nonincreasing.

 Passing from $Q$ to $\left|Q\right|$ preserves the constraint
$\left\|\left|Q\right|\right\|_p=1$ and $\left\|\left|Q\right|\right\|_2=\left\|Q\right\|_2$. Then it does not increase the energy functional by the pointwise inequality $\big|\left|Q(x)\right|-\left|Q(y)\right|\big|\le\left|Q(x)-Q(y)\right|$ and
the singular-integral representation \eqref{eq:Am-form},
\[
\left\langle A_{m}\left|Q\right|,\left|Q\right|\right\rangle
=\tfrac12\iint\big|\left|Q(x)\right|-\left|Q(y)\right|\big|^2 J_m(\left|x-y\right|)\,dx\,dy+m\left\|Q\right\|_2^2
\le\left\langle A_{m} Q,Q\right\rangle.
\]
Thus, we have  $B(\left|Q\right|)\le B(Q)=S$, and admissibility forces $B(\left|Q\right|)=S$. We may thus assume
$Q\ge0$.

 Let $Q^*$ be the symmetric-decreasing rearrangement of
$Q\ge0$. It preserves every $L^q$-norm, so $\left\|Q^*\right\|_p=1$ and $\left\|Q^*\right\|_2=\left\|Q\right\|_2$.
We claim the \emph{pseudo-relativistic P\'olya--Szeg\H{o} inequality}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:polya}
	\left\langle A_{m} Q^*,Q^*\right\rangle\le\left\langle A_{m} Q,Q\right\rangle.
\end{equation}

Firstly, by the singular-integral form \eqref{eq:Am-form}, we obtain
\[
\left\langle A_{m} u,u\right\rangle=\tfrac12\,\mathcal D[u]+m\left\|u\right\|_2^2,\qquad
\mathcal D[u]:=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2 J_m(\left|x-y\right|)\,dx\,dy .
\]
Since rearrangement preserves the mass term, $\left\|Q^*\right\|_2^2=\left\|Q\right\|_2^2$, inequality
\eqref{eq:polya} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diff-PS}
	\mathcal D[Q^*]\le\mathcal D[Q].
\end{equation}

Secondly, fix $\tau>0$ and each  $g_\tau$ is a symmetric-decreasing $L^1$ kernel, so the
rearrangement inequality of Frank--Seiringer \cite[Lem.~A.2]{FrankSeiringer}, applied with
the convex function $J(t)=t^2$ and the kernel $k=g_\tau$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:FS-tau}
	\mathcal D_\tau[Q^*]\le\mathcal D_\tau[Q],\qquad
	\mathcal D_\tau[u]:=\iint\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2 g_\tau(\left|x-y\right|)\,dx\,dy .
\end{equation}

Thirdly, The integrand
$(x,y,\tau)\mapsto\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2 g_\tau(\left|x-y\right|)$ is nonnegative and measurable, so by
Tonelli's theorem the order of integration may be exchanged. Using the Gaussian
superposition \eqref{eq:Jm-gauss}, we obtain
\begin{align}
	\mathcal D[u]
	&=\iint\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2 J_m(\left|x-y\right|)\,dx\,dy \notag\\ 
	&=\iint\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2\Big(\int_0^\infty g_\tau(\left|x-y\right|)\,d\mu_m(\tau)\Big)dx\,dy
	\label{eq:insert}\\    
	&=\int_0^\infty\Big(\iint\left|u(x)-u(y)\right|^2 g_\tau(\left|x-y\right|)\,dx\,dy\Big)d\mu_m(\tau)
	=\int_0^\infty\mathcal D_\tau[u]\,d\mu_m(\tau).   	\label{eq:tonelli}
\end{align}
Applying \eqref{eq:tonelli} to both $Q$ and $Q^*$ and using \eqref{eq:FS-tau} together
with $d\mu_m\ge0$, we have 
\[
\mathcal D[Q^*]=\int_0^\infty\mathcal D_\tau[Q^*]\,d\mu_m(\tau)
\le\int_0^\infty\mathcal D_\tau[Q]\,d\mu_m(\tau)=\mathcal D[Q],
\]
which is \eqref{eq:diff-PS}, hence \eqref{eq:polya}.

Consequently, $B(Q^*)=\left\langle A_{m} Q^*,Q^*\right\rangle+\left\|Q^*\right\|_2^2\le\left\langle A_{m} Q,Q\right\rangle+\left\|Q\right\|_2^2=B(Q)=S$.
Since $\left\|Q^*\right\|_p=1$ forces $B(Q^*)\ge S$, we get $B(Q^*)=S$. Thus $Q^*$ is a minimizer,
radial and radially nonincreasing, and we rename $Q:=Q^*$.

\medskip
\emph{Step 4.}
The minimizer $Q$ of \eqref{eq:Sinf} satisfies, with a Lagrange multiplier $\Lambda$, the
weak equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:EL}
	\left\langle A_{m} Q,\varphi\right\rangle+\left\langle Q,\varphi\right\rangle=\Lambda\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}Q^{p-1}\varphi ,
	\qquad\forall\,\varphi\inH^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).
\end{equation}
Testing \eqref{eq:EL} with $\varphi=Q$ and using $\left\|Q\right\|_p^p=1$ fixes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:multiplier}
	\Lambda=\left\langle A_{m} Q,Q\right\rangle+\left\|Q\right\|_2^2=B(Q)=S>0 .
\end{equation}
Thus $Q$ solves $(A_{m}+1)Q=\Lambda\,Q^{p-1}$ weakly.

\medskip
\emph{Step 5.}
Set $\widetilde Q:=\Lambda^{1/(p-2)}Q$. Using \eqref{eq:EL}, we obtain 
\[
(A_{m}+1)\widetilde Q=\Lambda^{1/(p-2)}(A_{m}+1)Q=\Lambda^{1/(p-2)}\Lambda\,Q^{p-1}
=\Lambda^{1+\frac1{p-2}}Q^{p-1},
\]
while $\widetilde Q^{\,p-1}=\Lambda^{(p-1)/(p-2)}Q^{p-1}$. Since
$1+\tfrac1{p-2}=\tfrac{p-1}{p-2}$, the two exponents coincide and
\[
(A_{m}+1)\widetilde Q=\widetilde Q^{\,p-1},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:norm} (with $\omega=1$).

\medskip
\emph{Step 6.}
Write $\widetilde Q=(A_{m}+1)^{-1}\widetilde Q^{\,p-1}=G_{m}*\widetilde Q^{\,p-1}$, with
$G_{m}>0$ the Green kernel of Proposition~\ref{prop:green}. As $\widetilde Q\ge0$,
$\widetilde Q\not\equiv0$ and $G_{m}>0$ everywhere, the convolution is strictly positive, so
$\widetilde Q>0$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. For strict monotonicity, $\widetilde Q^{\,p-1}$ is radial and
radially nonincreasing (inherited from $Q=Q^*$), and $G_{m}$ is radial and \emph{strictly}
decreasing. Hence,  for $\left|x_1\right|<\left|x_2\right|$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:strict-mono}
	\widetilde Q(x_1)-\widetilde Q(x_2)
	=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big(G_{m}(x_1-z)-G_{m}(x_2-z)\big)\,\widetilde Q(z)^{p-1}\,dz>0 .
\end{equation}
The positivity is not pointwise in $z$. It 
 follows from Riesz's rearrangement inequality,
which for the strictly decreasing radial kernel $G_{m}$ tested against the radial weight
$\widetilde Q^{\,p-1}$ gives
$\intG_{m}(x_1-z)\widetilde Q(z)^{p-1}dz>\intG_{m}(x_2-z)\widetilde Q(z)^{p-1}dz$ whenever
$\left|x_1\right|<\left|x_2\right|$ (strict since $G_{m}$ is strictly decreasing and
$\widetilde Q^{\,p-1}>0$ on a set of positive measure). Thus $\widetilde Q$ is radially
strictly decreasing.

\medskip
\emph{Step 7.}
It remains to show $\widetilde Q\in\mathcal G_m$, i.e.\ that $\widetilde Q$ minimizes the
action functional
\[
S_m(u)=\tfrac12 B(u)-\tfrac1p\left\|u\right\|_p^p
\]
over the Nehari manifold $\mathcal N_m=\{u\ne0:\ B(u)=\left\|u\right\|_p^p\}$ and to relate this
to \eqref{eq:wgn}. For $u\ne0$ consider the fibering map $t\mapsto S_m(tu)$, $t>0$.  It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fiber}
	S_m(tu)=\tfrac12\,t^2 B(u)-\tfrac1p\,t^p\left\|u\right\|_p^p,
	\qquad
	\frac{d}{dt}S_m(tu)=t\,B(u)-t^{p-1}\left\|u\right\|_p^p .
\end{equation}
The derivative vanishes at the unique
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tu}
	t_u=\Big(\frac{B(u)}{\left\|u\right\|_p^p}\Big)^{1/(p-2)}>0,
\end{equation}
which is the maximum of $S_m(tu)$ along $t>0$ and satisfies $t_u u\in\mathcal N_m$. Indeed, \begin{align*}
	B(t_uu)=t_u^2 B(u)=t_u^p\left\|u\right\|_p^p=\left\|t_uu\right\|_p^p.
\end{align*}
 Evaluating and using
 \begin{align*}
 	t_u^p\left\|u\right\|_p^p=t_u^2 B(u)=(B(u)/\left\|u\right\|_p^2)^{p/(p-2)},
 \end{align*}
 we obtain that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mNehari}
	S_m(t_uu)=\Big(\tfrac12-\tfrac1p\Big)t_u^p\left\|u\right\|_p^p
	=\Big(\tfrac12-\tfrac1p\Big)\Big(\frac{B(u)}{\left\|u\right\|_p^2}\Big)^{p/(p-2)}.
\end{equation}
Taking the infimum over $u\ne0$ and writing the Weinstein quotient
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weinstein-quot}
	S=\inf_{u\ne0}\frac{B(u)}{\left\|u\right\|_p^2},
\end{equation}
we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:level-relation}
	\inf_{\mathcal N_m}S_m=\Big(\tfrac12-\tfrac1p\Big)\,S^{\,p/(p-2)} .
\end{equation}
The \eqref{eq:weinstein-quot} coincides with the constrained infimum
\eqref{eq:Sinf}. Indeed, both $B$ and $\left\|\cdot\right\|_p^2$ are homogeneous of degree $2$, so
for $u\ne0$ and $t>0$,
\[
\frac{B(tu)}{\left\|tu\right\|_p^2}=\frac{t^2B(u)}{t^2\left\|u\right\|_p^2}=\frac{B(u)}{\left\|u\right\|_p^2},
\]
i.e.\ the quotient is constant along rays. Choosing $t=\left\|u\right\|_p^{-1}$ normalizes
$v:=u/\left\|u\right\|_p$ to $\left\|v\right\|_p=1$ and gives $B(u)/\left\|u\right\|_p^2=B(v)$. Conversely, every
admissible $v$ in \eqref{eq:Sinf} is of this form. Thus, we have
\[
\inf_{u\ne0}\frac{B(u)}{\left\|u\right\|_p^2}
=\inf_{\left\|v\right\|_p=1}B(v),
\]
which is \eqref{eq:Sinf}.

Since $Q$ attains $S$ in \eqref{eq:weinstein-quot} and $\widetilde Q$ is a positive
multiple of $Q$ lying on $\mathcal N_m$, $\widetilde Q$ attains
$\inf\limits_{\mathcal N_m}S_m$. Thus, $\widetilde Q\in\mathcal G_m$. Finally
\eqref{eq:weinstein-quot} is the reciprocal sharp constant in the
Weinstein--Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality \eqref{eq:wgn}: interpolating $\left\|u\right\|_p$
between the $B$-controlled $H^{1/2}$-norm and $\left\|u\right\|_2$ with exponent
$\theta=d(\tfrac12-\tfrac1p)$ gives
$\left\|u\right\|_p\le C_{m,p}\,B(u)^{\theta/2}\left\|u\right\|_2^{1-\theta}$, whose optimizers coincide,
up to a positive multiple and a dilation, with the minimizers of
\eqref{eq:weinstein-quot}, i.e.\ with $\widetilde Q$. This proves
Theorem~\ref{thm:existence}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:qual}
	Let $m\ge0$ and  $Q\in\mathcal G_{m}$. Then $Q>0$, $Q$ is radial and radially
	strictly decreasing, and $Q\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
From \eqref{eq:norm}, we know that 
	$Q=(A_{m}+1)^{-1}Q^{p-1}=G_{m}*Q^{p-1}$, where $G_{m}$ is positive, radial and strictly
	decreasing by Proposition~\ref{prop:green}. Since $Q\ge0$ and $Q\not\equiv0$, the
	convolution is strictly positive, so $Q>0$.  The convolution of a strictly decreasing
	radial kernel with a nonnegative radial function is strictly radially decreasing, so $Q$
	is radially strictly decreasing.
	
	Moser iteration applied to $(A_{m}+1)Q=Q^{p-1}$ gives
	$Q\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ \cite[Prop.~3.1]{CotiZelatiNolasco}. Interior Schauder estimates
	for $A_{m}$ \cite[Thm.~1.3]{StingaTorrea} and a bootstrap then yield $Q\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:pohozaev-derivation}
	Let $m\ge0$ and $Q\in\mathcal G_m$. Then
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:nehari-id}
		\left\langle A_{m} Q,Q\right\rangle+\left\|Q\right\|_2^2=\left\|Q\right\|_p^p ,
	\end{equation}
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pohozaev}
		\frac{d-1}{2}\,\left\langle A_{m} Q,Q\right\rangle-\frac{m^2}{2}\,\left\langle A_{m}^{-1}Q,Q\right\rangle
		+\frac d2\,\left\|Q\right\|_2^2=\frac dp\,\left\|Q\right\|_p^p .
	\end{equation}
	In particular, for $m=0$ the two identities decouple and give
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pohozaev-massless}
		\left\langle A_0 Q,Q\right\rangle=\vartheta\,\left\|Q\right\|_p^p,\qquad
		\left\|Q\right\|_2^2=(1-\vartheta)\,\left\|Q\right\|_p^p,\qquad
		\vartheta:=2d\Big(\tfrac12-\tfrac1p\Big)\in(0,1).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Testing \eqref{eq:norm} against $Q$ gives \eqref{eq:nehari-id}. Testing against
	$x\cdot\nabla Q$ and using the commutator identity
	$[A_{m},x\cdot\nabla]=-A_{m}+m^2A_{m}^{-1}$ (proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:comm}),
	\[
	\left\langle A_{m} Q,x\cdot\nabla Q\right\rangle
	=-\tfrac d2\left\langle A_{m} Q,Q\right\rangle+\tfrac12\left\langle (A_{m}-m^2A_{m}^{-1})Q,Q\right\rangle,
	\]
	together with $\left\langle Q,x\cdot\nabla Q\right\rangle=-\tfrac d2\left\|Q\right\|_2^2$ and
	$\left\langle Q^{p-1},x\cdot\nabla Q\right\rangle=-\tfrac dp\left\|Q\right\|_p^p$, yields \eqref{eq:pohozaev}. For
	$m=0$ the term $\left\langle A_{m}^{-1}Q,Q\right\rangle$ drops out; eliminating $\left\|Q\right\|_2^2$ between
	\eqref{eq:nehari-id} and \eqref{eq:pohozaev} gives
	$\left\langle A_0Q,Q\right\rangle=2d(\tfrac12-\tfrac1p)\left\|Q\right\|_p^p$, and then \eqref{eq:nehari-id} gives the
	second identity in \eqref{eq:pohozaev-massless}. Finally $\vartheta\in(0,1)$ is
	equivalent to $2<p<\frac{2d}{d-1}$, i.e.\ to \eqref{eq:range}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:decay}
	Let $m>0$ and $Q\in\mathcal G_m$. Then there are $C\ge1$ and $R\ge1$ with
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qdecay}
		C^{-1}\,\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|}\le Q(x)\le C\,\left|x\right|^{-\frac{d+1}{2}}e^{-m\left|x\right|},
		\qquad \left|x\right|\ge R,
	\end{equation}
	and, for every $m'<m$, there is $C_{m'}$ with
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qdecay-grad}
		\left|Q(x)\right|+\left|\nabla Q(x)\right|\le C_{m'}\,e^{-m'\left|x\right|}\qquad(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:qual}, we see that $Q\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and $Q(x)\to0$ as
	$\left|x\right|\to\infty$. Since $p>2$, the interval $\big(\tfrac{m}{p-1},m\big)$ is nonempty;
	fix once and for all
	\[
	m'\in\Big(\tfrac{m}{p-1},\,m\Big),
	\qquad\text{so that}\qquad
	m'':=(p-1)m'>m .
	\]
	Since $m'<m$, \eqref{eq:green-upper} gives
	\[
	\kappa:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}G_{m}(y)e^{m'\left|y\right|}\,dy<\infty ,
	\]
	and the function $W(x):=Ce^{-m'\left|x\right|}$ satisfies $(A_{m}+1)^{-1}W\le\kappa W$, i.e.
	\begin{align*}
		(A_{m}+1)W\ge\kappa^{-1}W .
	\end{align*}
	As $Q(x)\to0$ and $p>2$, we may fix $R_1$ with
	\begin{align*}
		(p-1)Q(x)^{p-2}\le\kappa^{-1}\qquad\text{for }\left|x\right|\ge R_1 ,
	\end{align*}
	and then choose $C$ so large that $W\ge Q$ on $\{\left|x\right|=R_1\}$ (possible since
	$Q\in L^\infty$). On $\{\left|x\right|\ge R_1\}$,
	\[
	(A_{m}+1)Q=Q^{p-1}=Q^{p-2}\cdot Q\le\tfrac{\kappa^{-1}}{p-1}\,Q\le\kappa^{-1}Q ,
	\]
	so the function $V:=W-Q$ satisfies
	\begin{align*}
		(A_{m}+1)V\ge\kappa^{-1}V\quad\text{on }\{\left|x\right|\ge R_1\},
		\qquad V\ge0\ \text{ on }\{\left|x\right|=R_1\},
	\end{align*}
	and $V(x)\to0$ as $\left|x\right|\to\infty$. The comparison principle for $A_{m}+1$, whose kernel
	$G_{m}$ is positive, gives $V\ge0$, that is
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qprelim}
		Q(x)\le C\,e^{-m'\left|x\right|},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
	\end{equation}
	
	Set $F:=Q^{p-1}\ge0$, $F\not\equiv0$. By \eqref{eq:Qprelim} we have
	$F(x)\le C^{p-1}e^{-m''\left|x\right|}$ with $m''>m$ by the choice of $m'$, and $F\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^{d})$.
	Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:convolution} with $H=G_{m}$, whose two-sided bound is
	\eqref{eq:green}, and this $F$ yields \eqref{eq:Qdecay}.
	
	Finally, interior Schauder estimates for $A_{m}+1$ \cite[Thm.~1.3]{StingaTorrea} applied to
	$(A_{m}+1)Q=Q^{p-1}$ on $B_1(x)$ give, using $Q\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{d})$,
	\[
	\left|\nabla Q(x)\right|\le C\Big(\sup_{B_2(x)}Q+\sup_{B_2(x)}Q^{p-1}\Big)\le C'\sup_{B_2(x)}Q ,
	\]
	and since $\left|y\right|\ge\left|x\right|-2$ for $y\in B_2(x)$, \eqref{eq:Qprelim} yields
	$$\sup\limits_{B_2(x)}Q\le Ce^{2m'}e^{-m'\left|x\right|} .$$ Hence
	$\left|\nabla Q(x)\right|\le C_{m'}e^{-m'\left|x\right|}$, which together with \eqref{eq:Qprelim} gives
	\eqref{eq:Qdecay-grad}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:ess-spec}
	Let $m>0$ and $Q\in\mathcal G_m$. Then
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:ess-spec}
		\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(L_{+})=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A_{m}+1)=[m+1,\infty),
		\qquad
		\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(L_{+})=m+1>0 .
	\end{equation}
	Consequently, the spectrum of $L_{+}$ in $(-\infty,m+1)$ consists of finitely many isolated
	eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, and every corresponding eigenfunction belongs to
	$L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and decays exponentially.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Firstly,	the operator $A_{m}+1$ is the Fourier multiplier with symbol
	$w(\xi)=\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}+1$, which is radial, continuous and strictly increasing in
	$\left|\xi\right|$, with $w(0)=m+1$ and $w(\xi)\to\infty$ as $\left|\xi\right|\to\infty$. Consequently
	$A_{m}+1$ has no eigenvalues: for $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, the level set $\{w=\lambda\}$ is contained
	in a sphere and hence has Lebesgue measure zero, so any solution of
	$(w-\lambda)\hat u=0$ in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ vanishes almost everywhere. The spectrum of a
	multiplier operator being the essential range of its symbol, we obtain
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:spec-free}
		\sigma(A_{m}+1)=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A_{m}+1)=\overline{w(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=[m+1,\infty).
	\end{equation}
	
	Write $L_{+}=(A_{m}+1)-V$ with $V:=(p-1)Q^{p-2}\ge0$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:qual}, we see
	that $V\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{d})$. It follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:decay} and $p>2$ that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:V-decay}
		\sup_{\left|x\right|\ge R}V(x)\le(p-1)\big(C_{m'}e^{-m'R}\big)^{p-2}\longrightarrow0
		\quad \text{as} \quad R\to\infty.
	\end{equation}
	
	{\bf\emph{Claim:}} $V(A_{m}+1)^{-1}$ is a compact operator on $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$.
	
	By \eqref{eq:spec-free}, we have $0\notin\sigma(A_{m}+1)$, so $(A_{m}+1)^{-1}$ is bounded on
	$L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$. Since it is the Fourier multiplier with symbol $1/w$ and
	$w(\xi)\ge w(0)=m+1$ for all $\xi$, Plancherel's theorem gives
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:resolvent-norm}
		\left\|(A_{m}+1)^{-1}u\right\|_{L^2}\le\frac{1}{m+1}\,\left\|u\right\|_{L^2},
		\qquad u\inL^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).
	\end{equation}
	Moreover, $(A_{m}+1)^{-1}$ gains one full derivative: for $u\inL^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and
	$v=(A_{m}+1)^{-1}u$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:gain}
		\left\|v\right\|_{H^1}^2=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1+\left|\xi\right|^2}{\big(\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}+1\big)^2}\,
		\left|\hat u(\xi)\right|^2\,d\xi\le C\left\|u\right\|_{L^2}^2 ,
	\end{equation}
	since the quotient in \eqref{eq:gain} is bounded on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ (it tends to $1$ as
	$\left|\xi\right|\to\infty$ and equals $(m+1)^{-2}$ at $\xi=0$). Thus
	$(A_{m}+1)^{-1}:L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to H^1(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ is bounded.
	
	We fix $R\ge1$ and split $V=V\mathbf 1_{B_R}+V\mathbf 1_{B_R^c}$, where
	$B_R=\{\left|x\right|<R\}$. Accordingly, we have
	\[
	V(A_{m}+1)^{-1}=T_R+S_R,\qquad
	T_R:=V\mathbf 1_{B_R}(A_{m}+1)^{-1},\quad
	S_R:=V\mathbf 1_{B_R^c}(A_{m}+1)^{-1}.
	\]
	
	Let $\{u_n\}$ be a bounded sequence in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$. By \eqref{eq:gain},
	$v_n:=(A_{m}+1)^{-1}u_n$ is bounded in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^{d})$, hence bounded in $H^1(B_R)$. Since
	$B_R$ is bounded, the Rellich--Kondrachov theorem provides a subsequence, still denoted
	$\{v_n\}$, and $v\inL^{2}(B_R)$ with $v_n\to v$ strongly in $L^{2}(B_R)$. As
	$V\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{d})$, we have
	\[
	\left\|T_Ru_n-V\mathbf 1_{B_R}v\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}
	=\left\|V\mathbf 1_{B_R}(v_n-v)\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}
	\le\left\|V\right\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\left\|v_n-v\right\|_{L^{2}(B_R)}\longrightarrow0 ,
	\]
	so $\{T_Ru_n\}$ has a convergent subsequence in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$. Hence $T_R$ is compact.
	
	On the other hand, for every $u\inL^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ with $\left\|u\right\|_{L^2}\le1$, it follows from
	\eqref{eq:resolvent-norm} that
	\begin{align*}
			\left\|V(A_{m}+1)^{-1}u-T_Ru\right\|_{L^2}=\left\|S_Ru\right\|_{L^2}
		&\le\Big(\sup_{\left|x\right|\ge R}V(x)\Big)\left\|(A_{m}+1)^{-1}u\right\|_{L^2}\\
		&\le\frac{1}{m+1}\sup_{\left|x\right|\ge R}V(x)=:\varepsilon_R ,
	\end{align*}
	and $\varepsilon_R\to0$ as $R\to\infty$ by \eqref{eq:V-decay}. Thus $T_R$ converges to
	$V(A_{m}+1)^{-1}$ in the operator norm of $\mathcal B(L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$. Each $T_R$ is compact,
	and a limit of compact operators in the operator norm is compact
	\cite[Thm.~VI.12]{ReedSimonI}. Hence, we obtain $V(A_{m}+1)^{-1}$ is compact, which proves the claim.
	
	Since $V$ is bounded, symmetric and, by the claim just proved, a relatively compact
	perturbation of $A_{m}+1$, Weyl's theorem on the invariance of the essential spectrum
	\cite[Thm.~XIII.14]{ReedSimonIV} gives
	\[
	\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(L_{+})=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}\big((A_{m}+1)-V\big)=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A_{m}+1)=[m+1,\infty),
	\]
	which together with \eqref{eq:spec-free} proves \eqref{eq:ess-spec}.
	
	Lastly, since $\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(L_{+})=m+1>0$, the spectrum of $L_{+}$ in $(-\infty,m+1)$ is purely
	discrete: it consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, which can only
	accumulate at $m+1$. In particular there are at most finitely many nonpositive
	eigenvalues, so the Morse index of $L_{+}$ is finite and any eigenvalue $\lambda<m+1$ has
	an eigenfunction in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$. The exponential decay of such eigenfunctions follows
	from the spectral gap $m+1-\lambda>0$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:ext-reg}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:morse}
	$L_{+}$ has Morse index one on $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$. In particular, its restriction to $L^{2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$
	has Morse index one.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Recall that the Morse index of $L_{+}$ is the maximal dimension of a subspace of
	$H^{1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ on which the bilinear form $\left\langle L_{+}\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle$ is negative definite. By
	Proposition~\ref{prop:ess-spec}, it is finite and equals the number of negative
	eigenvalues of $L_{+}$, counted with multiplicity.
	
Firstly, we show the Morse index is at least one. Applying $L_{+}$ to $Q$ and using
	\eqref{eq:norm}, we obtain
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:LplusQ}
		L_{+} Q=A_{m} Q+Q-(p-1)Q^{p-1}=-(p-2)Q^{p-1},
	\end{equation}
	which implies that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:LplusQQ}
		\left\langle L_{+} Q,Q\right\rangle=-(p-2)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}Q^{p}\,dx=-(p-2)\left\|Q\right\|_p^p<0 ,
	\end{equation}
	since $p>2$ and $Q>0$. Thus, we have $\left\langle L_{+}\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle$ is negative on the one-dimensional
	space $\mathrm{span}\{Q\}$, and the Morse index is at least one. Note that $Q$ is radial,
	so the same conclusion holds for the restriction of $L_{+}$ to $L^{2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$.
	
Secondly, we will show	the Morse index is at most one. From Theorem~\ref{thm:existence},  the  minimum $S_m$ can be attained by  minimizes $Q$   on the Nehari manifold $\mathcal N_m=\{u\ne0:\ B(u)=\left\|u\right\|_p^p\}$, which is
	a $C^2$ hypersurface near $Q$ with tangent space
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:tangent-space}
		T_Q\mathcal N_m=\Big\{\xi\inH^{1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}):\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}Q^{p-1}\xi\,dx=0\Big\}.
	\end{equation}
	Indeed, setting $K(u):=B(u)-\left\|u\right\|_p^p$ for the constraint function, for
	$\xi\inH^{1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$, we have 
	\[
	\left\langle K'(Q),\xi\right\rangle=2\left\langle (A_{m}+1)Q,\xi\right\rangle-p\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}Q^{p-1}\xi
	=(2-p)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}Q^{p-1}\xi ,
	\]
	where we used the fact $(A_{m}+1)Q=Q^{p-1}$. In particular,
	\begin{align*}
		\left\langle K'(Q),Q\right\rangle=(2-p)\left\|Q\right\|_p^p\ne0,
	\end{align*} so $K'(Q)\ne0$ and \eqref{eq:tangent-space} holds.
	
	Since $Q$ is a constrained minimizer, the second variation of $S_m$ at $Q$ is
	nonnegative on $T_Q\mathcal N_m$. As $S_m''(Q)=L_{+}$, this shows
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:posdef-tangent}
		\left\langle L_{+}\xi,\xi\right\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for all }\xi\in T_Q\mathcal N_m .
	\end{equation}
	
	Suppose now that there were a two-dimensional subspace $E\subsetH^{1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ on which
	$\left\langle L_{+}\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle$ is negative definite. Since $T_Q\mathcal N_m$ has codimension one and
	$E\cap T_Q\mathcal N_m\ne\{0\}$, so there exists $\xi\ne0$ with
	$\left\langle L_{+}\xi,\xi\right\rangle<0$ and $\xi\in T_Q\mathcal N_m$, contradicting
	\eqref{eq:posdef-tangent}. Hence, the Morse index is at most one.
	We conclude that the Morse index of $L_{+}$ equals one.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:ext}
For $u\inH^{1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ the boundary value problem
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ext-bvp}
\Delta_x U+\partial_{yy}U-m^2U=0\ \text{in }\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+},\qquad U(\cdot,0)=u,\qquad
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\!\big(\left|\nabla U\right|^2+m^2U^2\big)<\infty,
\end{equation}
has a unique solution $U=\mathcal{U} u$, given in Fourier variables by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ext-fourier}
\widehat U(\xi,y)=\hat u(\xi)\,e^{-y\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}},
\end{equation}
and by the Poisson formula $U(x,y)=(P^m_y*u)(x)$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:poisson}
P^m_y(x)=c_d\,m^{\frac{d+1}{2}}\,y\,
\frac{\mathcal{K}_{\frac{d+1}{2}}\!\big(m\sqrt{\left|x\right|^2+y^2}\big)}
{(\left|x\right|^2+y^2)^{\frac{d+1}{4}}}\;>\;0 .
\end{equation}
It satisfies the Dirichlet--Neumann relation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:DtN}
-\partial_yU(\cdot,0)=A_{m} u\quad\text{in }H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),
\end{equation}
and the trace energy identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trace-energy}
\left\langle A_{m} u,u\right\rangle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\!\big(\left|\nabla \mathcal{U} u\right|^2+m^2(\mathcal{U} u)^2\big)
=\min_{V|_{y=0}=u}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\!\big(\left|\nabla V\right|^2+m^2V^2\big).
\end{equation}
The minimizer is unique by strict convexity of the extension functional.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We	write $\omega(\xi):=\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}$, so that $A_{m}$ has Fourier symbol $\omega$.
	
	\emph{Step 1: the Fourier-side solution \eqref{eq:ext-fourier}.}
	Taking the Fourier transform in $x$ turns $\Delta_x$ into multiplication by $-\left|\xi\right|^2$,
	so \eqref{eq:ext-bvp} becomes, for each fixed $\xi$, the ordinary differential equation in
	$y$
	\[
	\partial_{yy}\widehat U(\xi,y)=(\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2)\widehat U(\xi,y)=\omega(\xi)^2\widehat U(\xi,y),
	\qquad \widehat U(\xi,0)=\hat u(\xi).
	\]
	Its general solution is 
	$$\widehat U=A(\xi)e^{-y\omega}+B(\xi)e^{+y\omega}.$$
	The finite-energy	condition 
	$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}(\left|\nabla U\right|^2+m^2U^2)<\infty$$ forces $B\equiv0$, since
	$e^{+y\omega}$ grows exponentially and would render the $y$-integral infinite. The boundary
	condition then gives $A=\hat u$. Thus, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:ext-fourier-1}
		\widehat U(\xi,y)=\hat u(\xi)\,e^{-y\omega(\xi)},
	\end{equation}
	which is the unique finite-energy solution of \eqref{eq:ext-bvp}.
	
	\emph{Step 2: the trace energy identity \eqref{eq:trace-energy}.}
	By Plancherel's theorem and  \eqref{eq:ext-fourier-1}, we obtain 
	 \begin{align*}
	 	\left|\nabla U\right|^2=\left|\partial_yU\right|^2+\left|\nabla_xU\right|^2 \quad \text{and}	 \quad \partial_y\widehat U=-\omega\hat ue^{-y\omega},
	 \end{align*}
which implies that
	\begin{align*}
		\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\big(\left|\nabla U\right|^2+m^2U^2\big)
		&=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\int_0^\infty\big(\omega^2+\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2\big)\left|\hat u(\xi)\right|^2e^{-2y\omega}\,dy\,d\xi\\
		&=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\omega^2+\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}{2\omega}\left|\hat u(\xi)\right|^2\,d\xi\\
		&	=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\omega\left|\hat u\right|^2\,d\xi=\left\langle A_{m} u,u\right\rangle.
	\end{align*}
                                                                                              
Then,the first equality in \eqref{eq:trace-energy} is proved.
	
	\emph{Step 3: the minimality in \eqref{eq:trace-energy}.}
	The bilinear form  $$E(V):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}(\left|\nabla V\right|^2+m^2V^2)$$ is  nonnegative, which is convex  on the affine space $\mathcal A_u:=\{V:V|_{y=0}=u,\ E(V)<\infty\}$. 
	
	It is in	fact strictly convex: by the direct calculation,   for $V_0,V_1\in\mathcal A_u$, we have 
	\[
	E\Big(\tfrac{V_0+V_1}{2}\Big)=\tfrac12E(V_0)+\tfrac12E(V_1)-\tfrac14E(V_0-V_1),
	\]
	and $V_0-V_1$ vanishes on $\{y=0\}$, so $E(V_0-V_1)>0$ unless $V_0=V_1$. Thus $E$ has at
	most one minimizer on $\mathcal A_u$. Since $E$ is
	coercive and weakly lower semicontinuous, we obtain the  existence of  minimizer. If $V_*$ is the minimizer, then, for every
	$\varphi$ with $\varphi|_{y=0}=0$, we have
	\[
	0=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}E(V_*+t\varphi)
	=2\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\big(\nabla V_*\cdot\nabla\varphi+m^2V_*\varphi\big)
	=2\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\big(-\Delta V_*+m^2V_*\big)\varphi ,
	\]
where	the last step by integration by parts, the boundary term vanishes since
	$\varphi|_{y=0}=0$. As $\varphi$ is arbitrary, we have
	\begin{align*}
		-\Delta V_*+m^2V_*=0 \quad \text{with} \quad 	V_*|_{y=0}=u
	\end{align*} 
 and $E(V_*)<\infty$. By the uniqueness in Step~1, we have $V_*=\mathcal{U} u$. Hence the
	extension $\mathcal{U} u$ is the unique minimizer, and by Step~2 the minimum value equals
	$\left\langle A_{m} u,u\right\rangle$, proving \eqref{eq:trace-energy}.
	
	\emph{Step 4: the Dirichlet--Neumann relation \eqref{eq:DtN}.}
	Differentiating \eqref{eq:ext-fourier} in $y$ and setting $y=0$, we have 
	\[
	-\partial_y\widehat U(\xi,0)=\omega(\xi)\hat u(\xi)=\widehat{A_{m} u}(\xi),
	\]
	so $-\partial_yU(\cdot,0)=A_{m} u$ in $H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$, which is \eqref{eq:DtN}.
	
	\emph{Step 5: the Poisson kernel \eqref{eq:poisson}.}
	By \eqref{eq:ext-fourier} and the convolution theorem, we have 
	\[
U(\cdot,y)=P^m_y*u \quad \text{with} \quad	P^m_y:=\mathcal F^{-1}_\xi\big[e^{-y\omega(\xi)}\big]
	=\mathcal F^{-1}_\xi\big[e^{-y\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}}\big].
	\]
	The inverse Fourier transform of the radial function $e^{-y\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}}$ is
	classical and yields the Bessel form \eqref{eq:poisson}; see Stinga--Torrea
	\cite[Thm.~1.1]{StingaTorrea} (the case $s=\tfrac12$ of the $(-\Delta+m^2)^s$-extension,
	for which the weight $y^{1-2s}\equiv1$) and \cite[\S7.11]{LiebLoss}. Since
	$\mathcal K_{\frac{d+1}{2}}>0$ and all remaining factors in \eqref{eq:poisson} are
	positive, $P^m_y>0$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:ext-reg}
Let $L\phi=\lambda\phi$ with $\phi\inL^{2}_{\mathrm{rad}}$, $\lambda<m+W_\infty$, and $\Phi=\mathcal{U}\phi$. Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\Phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+})$;
\item $\phi\in C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ for some $\alpha\in(0,1)$, and
$\Phi\in C^{1,\alpha}\big(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\cap(K\times[0,1])\big)$ for every compact
$K\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$; in particular $\partial_y\Phi(\cdot,0)$ exists pointwise;
\item for every $m'<m$ there is $C$ with
$\left|\Phi(x,y)\right|+\left|\nabla\Phi(x,y)\right|\le C\,e^{-m'\varrho}$, $\varrho=\sqrt{\left|x\right|^2+y^2}$;
\item there is $c>0$ with $\Phi(x,y)\ge c\,e^{-m\varrho}\varrho^{-d/2}$ for $\varrho\ge1$
when $\phi>0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
\emph{(i)} The equation $\Delta_{x,y}\Phi=m^2\Phi$ is linear elliptic with constant
	coefficients, so $\Phi$ is real-analytic in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}$; in particular
	$\Phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+})$.
	
	\emph{(ii)} From \eqref{eq:DtN} and $L\phi=\lambda\phi$, we have
	\[
	(A_{m}+1)\phi=(1+\lambda-W)\phi ,
	\qquad
	\phi=(A_{m}+1)^{-1}\big[(1+\lambda-W)\phi\big]=G_{m}*\big[(1+\lambda-W)\phi\big].
	\]
	Since $\phi\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and $W\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{d})$, Moser iteration
	\cite[Prop.~3.1]{CotiZelatiNolasco} gives $\phi\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$;
	bootstrap in the above convolution representation, together with standard H\"older
	estimates for the Green kernel $G_{m}$, yields
	$\phi\in C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ for some $\alpha\in(0,1)$. The Neumann datum
	$-\partial_y\Phi(\cdot,0)=(\lambda-W)\phi$ then belongs to
	$C^{0,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$.
	
	 As $s=\tfrac12$, the extension weight $y^{1-2s}$
	reduces to $1$, so the boundary Neumann problem has constant coefficients, and Schauder
	theory \cite[Thm.~1.3]{StingaTorrea} gives
	$\Phi\in C^{1,\alpha}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\cap(K\times[0,1]))$ for every compact
	$K\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$. In particular, $\partial_y\Phi(\cdot,0)$ exists pointwise.
	
\emph{(iii) Decay.}
We first establish the exponential decay of the boundary trace $\phi$, and then propagate
it to $\Phi$ and $\nabla\Phi$ through a weighted energy estimate of Agmon type on the
extension.

\emph{Step 1: decay of the trace.}
We claim that for every $m'<m$ there is a constant $C_{m'}>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:phi-decay-weak}
	\left|\phi(x)\right|\le C_{m'}e^{-m'\left|x\right|}\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:DtN} and $L\phi=\lambda\phi$, the trace satisfies
$\phi=G_{m}*\big[(1+\lambda-W)\phi\big]$. Since $\phi(x)\to0$ and $W(x)\to W_\infty$ as
$\left|x\right|\to\infty$, we may fix $R_1$ such that $\left|1+\lambda-W(x)\right|\le\kappa^{-1}$ for
$\left|x\right|\ge R_1$, where $\kappa:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}G_{m}(y)e^{m'\left|y\right|}\,dy$ is finite because $m'<m$,
by \eqref{eq:green-upper}. The comparison function $W_1:=Ce^{-m'\left|x\right|}$ then satisfies
$(A_{m}+1)^{-1}W_1\le\kappa W_1$, that is $(A_{m}+1)W_1\ge\kappa^{-1}W_1$ on $\{\left|x\right|\ge R_1\}$.
Choosing $C$ large enough that $W_1\ge\phi$ on $\{\left|x\right|=R_1\}$, the comparison principle
for $A_{m}+1$, whose kernel $G_{m}$ is positive, yields \eqref{eq:phi-decay-weak}.

\emph{Step 2: a weighted energy bound.}
Fix $m'<m$ with $2m'^2<m^2$, and write $\varrho=\sqrt{\left|x\right|^2+y^2}$. For $R\ge1$ we
introduce the bounded Lipschitz weight
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trunc-weight}
	\zeta_R:=\min\big(e^{m'\varrho},\,R\big),
\end{equation}
which satisfies $0\le\zeta_R\le R$ and $\left|\nabla\zeta_R\right|\le m'\zeta_R$ almost
everywhere. The gradient bound holds because $\left|\nabla\varrho\right|=1$ on the set where
$\zeta_R=e^{m'\varrho}$, while $\nabla\zeta_R=0$ on the set where $\zeta_R=R$. Since
$\Phi\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+})$ by the finite extension energy and $\zeta_R$ is bounded and Lipschitz,
the product $\zeta_R^2\Phi$ belongs to $H^1(\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+})$ and is admissible as a test function in
the weak form of $\Delta_{x,y}\Phi=m^2\Phi$ with Neumann datum
$-\partial_y\Phi(\cdot,0)=(\lambda-W)\phi$. Testing against $\zeta_R^2\Phi$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-energy}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\nabla\Phi\cdot\nabla\big(\zeta_R^2\Phi\big)
	+m^2\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\Phi^2\zeta_R^2
	=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(\lambda-W)\phi\,\zeta_R^2\Phi\big|_{y=0}\,dx.
\end{equation}
Expanding $\nabla(\zeta_R^2\Phi)=\zeta_R^2\nabla\Phi+2\zeta_R\Phi\,\nabla\zeta_R$ and using
$\left|\nabla\zeta_R\right|\le m'\zeta_R$ together with Young's inequality,
\[
2\big|\zeta_R\Phi\,\nabla\zeta_R\cdot\nabla\Phi\big|
\le 2m'\zeta_R^2\left|\Phi\right|\left|\nabla\Phi\right|
\le\tfrac12\zeta_R^2\left|\nabla\Phi\right|^2+2m'^2\zeta_R^2\Phi^2.
\]
Absorbing the gradient term into the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:weighted-energy}, we
obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absorbed}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\Big(\tfrac12\left|\nabla\Phi\right|^2+\big(m^2-2m'^2\big)\Phi^2\Big)\zeta_R^2
	\le\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left|\lambda-W\right|\,\left|\phi\right|\,\zeta_R^2\,\left|\Phi\right|\big|_{y=0}\,dx.
\end{equation}
For the boundary term, Cauchy--Schwarz and the boundedness of $\lambda-W$ give, with
$\Phi\big|_{y=0}=\phi$,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left|\lambda-W\right|\,\left|\phi\right|\,\zeta_R^2\,\left|\phi\right|\,dx
\le C\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\zeta_R^2\left|\phi\right|^2\,dx.
\]
Now choose $m''\in(m',m)$. Applying Step~1 with the exponent $m''$ yields
$\left|\phi(x)\right|\le C_{m''}e^{-m''\left|x\right|}$, while on the boundary
$\zeta_R\big|_{y=0}\le e^{m'\left|x\right|}$. Hence
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\zeta_R^2\left|\phi\right|^2\,dx
\le C_{m''}^2\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{2m'\left|x\right|}e^{-2m''\left|x\right|}\,dx
=C_{m''}^2\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-2(m''-m')\left|x\right|}\,dx=:C_{m',m''},
\]
which is finite because $m''>m'$, and independent of $R$. Since $2m'^2<m^2$, the
left-hand side of \eqref{eq:absorbed} controls
$\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\big(\left|\nabla\Phi\right|^2+\Phi^2\big)\zeta_R^2$, so that
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\big(\left|\nabla\Phi\right|^2+\Phi^2\big)\zeta_R^2\le C_{m'}
\qquad\text{for all }R\ge1.
\]
As $R\to\infty$, the weights $\zeta_R^2$ increase monotonically to $e^{2m'\varrho}$, so the
monotone convergence theorem gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-H1}
	\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\big(\left|\nabla\Phi\right|^2+\Phi^2\big)e^{2m'\varrho}\,dx\,dy\le C_{m'}.
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 3: from weighted energy to pointwise decay.}
Since $\Phi$ solves the constant-coefficient elliptic equation
$\Delta_{x,y}\Phi=m^2\Phi$, interior elliptic estimates on a unit ball
$B_1(x_0,y_0)\subset\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}$, together with the boundary $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity of (ii)
when $y_0<1$, give
\[
\left|\Phi(x_0,y_0)\right|+\left|\nabla\Phi(x_0,y_0)\right|
\le C\bigg(\int_{B_1(x_0,y_0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\big(\left|\nabla\Phi\right|^2+\Phi^2\big)\bigg)^{1/2}.
\]
On $B_1(x_0,y_0)$ we have $\varrho\ge\varrho_0-1$ with
$\varrho_0=\sqrt{\left|x_0\right|^2+y_0^2}$. Multiplying the previous inequality by
$e^{m'\varrho_0}$ and using \eqref{eq:weighted-H1},
\[
e^{m'\varrho_0}\Big(\left|\Phi(x_0,y_0)\right|+\left|\nabla\Phi(x_0,y_0)\right|\Big)
\le Ce^{m'}\bigg(\int_{B_1(x_0,y_0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}
\big(\left|\nabla\Phi\right|^2+\Phi^2\big)e^{2m'\varrho}\bigg)^{1/2}\le C_{m'}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\left|\Phi(x,y)\right|+\left|\nabla\Phi(x,y)\right|\le C_{m'}e^{-m'\varrho}
\qquad\text{for }(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+},
\]
which is the assertion of (iii) for every $m'<m/\sqrt2$. Any smaller decay rate follows a
fortiori, and the range may be extended to all $m'<m$ by iterating
\eqref{eq:weighted-H1} over dyadic shells.

	\emph{(iv)} Suppose $\phi>0$. Since $P^m_y>0$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:ext} and
	$\phi>0$,
	\[
	\Phi(x,y)=(P^m_y*\phi)(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}P^m_y(x-x')\phi(x')\,dx'>0
	\qquad\text{pointwise on }\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}.
	\]
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:phi1pos}
The lowest radial eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ of $L=A_{m}+W$ (with $W$ radial, bounded,
$W(\infty)=W_\infty$) is simple, and its eigenfunction may be chosen with $\phi_1>0$ on
$[0,\infty)$; consequently $\Phi_1=\mathcal{U}\phi_1>0$ on $\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:trace-energy},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:la1-var}
\lambda_1=\min_{\substack{U\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{rad}}\\ U_0\not\equiv0}}
\frac{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}(\left|\nabla U\right|^2+m^2U^2)+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}W\,U_0^2}
{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}U_0^2},\qquad U_0:=U|_{y=0},
\end{equation}
over $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{rad}}=\{U:U\ \text{$x$-radial, numerator and denominator finite}\}$.
Since $\left|\nabla\left|U\right|\right|=\left|\nabla U\right|$ and $U_0^2=\left|U_0\right|^2$ a.e., $\left|\Phi_1\right|$ is
also a minimizer, so we may take $\Phi_1\ge0$. The Euler--Lagrange equations are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:phi1-EL}
\Delta_{x,y}\Phi_1=m^2\Phi_1\ (\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}),\qquad
-\partial_y\Phi_1(\cdot,0)+W\phi_1=\lambda_1\phi_1 .
\end{equation}
Internally $\Delta_{x,y}\Phi_1=m^2\Phi_1\ge0$, and $\Phi_1\ge0$, $\not\equiv0$, so the
strong maximum principle gives $\Phi_1>0$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}$. If $\phi_1(x_0)=0$ for some
$x_0\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, then $(x_0,0)$ is a boundary minimum of $\Phi_1$ with value $0$; the Hopf
boundary point lemma gives $-\partial_y\Phi_1(x_0,0)>0$, contradicting
\eqref{eq:phi1-EL} which yields $-\partial_y\Phi_1(x_0,0)=(\lambda_1-W(x_0))\phi_1(x_0)=0$.
Hence $\phi_1>0$. Simplicity: two positive minimizers $\Phi,\Phi'$ and the sliding
$\Psi_t=\Phi-t\Phi'$, $t^*=\inf\{t:\Psi_t\not>0\}$, give a nonnegative minimizer
$\Psi_{t^*}$ which, if $\not\equiv0$, is $>0$ by Hopf, contradicting the definition of
$t^*$; so $\Phi=t^*\Phi'$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:ratio}
$\Xi$ satisfies, in the weak sense on $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{rad}}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Xieq}
\operatorname{div}\!\big(\Phi_1^2\nabla\Xi\big)=0\ \text{in }\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+},\qquad
-\Phi_1^2\,\partial_y\Xi\big|_{y=0}=\mu\,\phi_1^2\,\Xi_0 .
\end{equation}
Neither $m$ nor $W$ appears in \eqref{eq:Xieq}; both are encoded in the weight
$\Phi_1^2>0$ and $\rho:=\phi_1^2>0$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
\emph{Interior identity.} With $\Phi_2=\Phi_1\Xi$,
$\nabla\Phi_2=\Xi\nabla\Phi_1+\Phi_1\nabla\Xi$ and
$\Delta\Phi_2=\Xi\Delta\Phi_1+2\nabla\Phi_1\cdot\nabla\Xi+\Phi_1\Delta\Xi$, where
$\Delta=\Delta_{x,y}$. Using $\Delta\Phi_j=m^2\Phi_j$,
\[
m^2\Phi_1\Xi=\Xi m^2\Phi_1+2\nabla\Phi_1\cdot\nabla\Xi+\Phi_1\Delta\Xi
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\Phi_1\Delta\Xi+2\nabla\Phi_1\cdot\nabla\Xi=0 .
\]
Multiplying by $\Phi_1$ gives
$\Phi_1^2\Delta\Xi+2\Phi_1\nabla\Phi_1\cdot\nabla\Xi=\operatorname{div}(\Phi_1^2\nabla\Xi)=0$; the
$m^2$ terms cancelled exactly.

\emph{Boundary identity.} At $y=0$,
$\Phi_1^2\partial_y\Xi|_0=(\partial_y\Phi_2\cdot\Phi_1-\Phi_2\partial_y\Phi_1)|_0$. By the
Neumann relations $\partial_y\Phi_j|_0=-(\lambda_j-W)\phi_j$ (from \eqref{eq:DtN} and
$L\phi_j=\lambda_j\phi_j$),
\[
\Phi_1^2\partial_y\Xi|_0
=-(\lambda_2-W)\phi_2\,\phi_1+(\lambda_1-W)\phi_1\,\phi_2
=-(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)\phi_1\phi_2=-\mu\,\phi_1^2\,\Xi_0 .
\]
Hence $-\Phi_1^2\partial_y\Xi|_0=\mu\phi_1^2\Xi_0$. The weak formulation follows by
testing with $\Phi_1\varphi$ and the integration by parts of
Proposition~\ref{prop:key-IBP}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:key-IBP}
For $V\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{rad}}$ set $U=\Phi_1 V$. Then, with
$\mathfrak{a}[V]:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\Phi_1^2\left|\nabla V\right|^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:key-IBP}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\!\big(\left|\nabla U\right|^2+m^2U^2\big)+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}W\,U_0^2
-\lambda_1\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}U_0^2
=\mathfrak{a}[V].
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Expand $\left|\nabla U\right|^2=\left|V\nabla\Phi_1+\Phi_1\nabla V\right|^2
=V^2\left|\nabla\Phi_1\right|^2+2V\Phi_1\,\nabla\Phi_1\cdot\nabla V+\Phi_1^2\left|\nabla V\right|^2$.
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:IBP-1}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\!\big(\left|\nabla U\right|^2+m^2U^2\big)
=\mathfrak{a}[V]
+\underbrace{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\!\big(V^2\left|\nabla\Phi_1\right|^2
+2V\Phi_1\nabla\Phi_1\!\cdot\!\nabla V+m^2\Phi_1^2V^2\big)}_{=:I}.
\end{equation}
For the cross term, $2V\Phi_1\nabla\Phi_1\cdot\nabla V
=\Phi_1\,\nabla\Phi_1\cdot\nabla(V^2)$, and integrating by parts in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}$ (the decay
Proposition~\ref{prop:ext-reg}(iii) kills the contribution at $\varrho=\infty$),
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\Phi_1\,\nabla\Phi_1\cdot\nabla(V^2)
=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}V^2\,\operatorname{div}(\Phi_1\nabla\Phi_1)
+\int_{\{y=0\}}V_0^2\,\big(-\Phi_1\partial_y\Phi_1\big)\big|_0 .
\]
Now $\operatorname{div}(\Phi_1\nabla\Phi_1)=\left|\nabla\Phi_1\right|^2+\Phi_1\Delta\Phi_1
=\left|\nabla\Phi_1\right|^2+m^2\Phi_1^2$. Substituting,
\[
I=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\!\big(V^2\left|\nabla\Phi_1\right|^2+m^2\Phi_1^2V^2\big)
-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}V^2\big(\left|\nabla\Phi_1\right|^2+m^2\Phi_1^2\big)
+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V_0^2(-\Phi_1\partial_y\Phi_1)|_0 ,
\]
and the two interior integrals cancel identically, leaving
\[
I=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V_0^2\,\big(-\Phi_1\partial_y\Phi_1\big)\big|_0
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V_0^2\,\phi_1\,(\lambda_1-W)\phi_1
=\lambda_1\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\phi_1^2V_0^2-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}W\phi_1^2V_0^2 ,
\]
using $-\partial_y\Phi_1|_0=(\lambda_1-W)\phi_1$. Since $U_0^2=\phi_1^2V_0^2$, this reads
$I=\lambda_1\left\|U_0\right\|_2^2-\int W U_0^2$. Inserting into \eqref{eq:IBP-1} and rearranging
gives \eqref{eq:key-IBP}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{prop:key-IBP} is the analytic core of the paper: it converts the
massive, potential-bearing quadratic form $\left\langle (L-\lambda_1)u,u\right\rangle$ into the massless,
potential-free weighted Dirichlet energy $\mathfrak{a}[V]$, at the price of the weight
$\Phi_1^2$. The cancellation of the interior term is exact and uses only the extension
equation $\Delta\Phi_1=m^2\Phi_1$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:trace-compact}
The trace $\mathcal T:\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{rad}\toL^{2}(\rho\,dx)$, $V\mapsto V_0$, is well-defined,
bounded and compact. Consequently the weighted Dirichlet--Neumann (Steklov) operator
$\Lambda_a$ is self-adjoint, nonnegative, with purely discrete spectrum
$0=\nu_0<\nu_1\le\nu_2\le\cdots\to\infty$, $\nu_0$ simple with eigenfunction
$g_0\equiv\mathrm{const}$, and the min--max characterization holds:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:minmax}
\nu_k=\min_{\substack{\mathcal E\subset\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{rad}\\ \dim\mathcal E=k+1}}
\ \max_{0\ne V\in\mathcal E}\mathcal R[V].
\end{equation}
Each level is attained; a minimizer $V^{(k)}$ satisfies the weak eigenvalue equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:steklov-weak}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}a\,\nabla V^{(k)}\cdot\nabla\varphi
=\nu_k\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\rho\,g_k\,\varphi_0,\qquad
\forall\varphi\in\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{rad},\quad g_k:=V^{(k)}_0 .
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
\emph{Trace inequality.} Integrating by parts,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Phi_1^2 V_0^2=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\partial_y(\Phi_1^2 V^2)
=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\big(2\Phi_1\partial_y\Phi_1\,V^2+2\Phi_1^2V\partial_yV\big).
\]
Since $\left|\partial_y\Phi_1\right|\le C\Phi_1$ (Prop.~\ref{prop:ext-reg}(iii)), Young's
inequality gives $\int\rho V_0^2\le C\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}\Phi_1^2(\left|\nabla V\right|^2+V^2)
\le C\left\|V\right\|_\mathcal{V}^2$. \emph{Compactness.} Let $V^{(n)}\rightharpoonup0$ in $\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{rad}$. For
$\left|x\right|>R$ the exterior extension energy controls the exterior trace with a constant that
vanishes as $R\to\infty$ (exponential weight $\Phi_1^2$), so the tail is uniformly small;
on $\{\left|x\right|<R\}$, the trace is bounded in $H^{1/2}(B_R)$ and
$H^{1/2}(B_R)\hookrightarrow\hookrightarrow L^2(B_R)$ compactly, so $V_0^{(n)}\to0$
strongly there. Hence $\mathcal T$ is compact. Discreteness and \eqref{eq:minmax} follow
from the spectral theorem for the nonnegative self-adjoint $\Lambda_a$ with compact
resolvent. The value $\nu_0=0$ is attained by $V\equiv1$ and is simple because $a>0$ is
connected: $\mathfrak{a}[V]=0\Rightarrow V$ constant.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:spectral-corr}
Let $\{\lambda_k\}_{k\ge1}$ be the radial eigenvalues of $L=A_{m}+W$ below
$\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(L)=m+W_\infty$, listed with multiplicity, and $\{\nu_k\}_{k\ge0}$ the Steklov
eigenvalues of $\Lambda_a$ (with $a=\Phi_1^2$, $\rho=\phi_1^2$). Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr}
\nu_k=\lambda_{k+1}-\lambda_1\qquad(k=0,1,2,\dots),
\end{equation}
and the map $\phi\mapsto V:=\mathcal{U}\phi/\Phi_1$ is a bijection between the radial
eigenspace of $L$ at $\lambda_{k+1}$ and the Steklov eigenspace of $\Lambda_a$ at $\nu_k$,
preserving multiplicities.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $u\inH^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}$, $U=\mathcal{U} u$, $V=U/\Phi_1$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:key-IBP},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-quad}
\left\langle (L-\lambda_1)u,u\right\rangle=\mathfrak{a}[V],\qquad
\left\|u\right\|_2^2=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\phi_1^2 V_0^2=\left\|V_0\right\|_\rho^2 .
\end{equation}
The map $u\mapsto V$ is a linear isomorphism $H^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}\to\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{rad}$ (inverse $V\mapsto\phi_1 V_0$
at the boundary, $U=\Phi_1 V$ in the bulk), because $\Phi_1>0$ is smooth with controlled
decay, and it intertwines the two quadratic-form pairs in \eqref{eq:corr-quad}. By the
min--max principle applied to both sides,
\[
\lambda_{k+1}-\lambda_1=\min_{\dim\mathcal F=k+1}\max_{u\in\mathcal F}
\frac{\left\langle (L-\lambda_1)u,u\right\rangle}{\left\|u\right\|_2^2}
=\min_{\dim\mathcal E=k+1}\max_{V\in\mathcal E}\mathcal R[V]=\nu_k ,
\]
proving \eqref{eq:corr}. The eigenspace correspondence follows because $Lu=\lambda_{k+1}u$
transforms, under $u=\phi_1 V_0$, $U=\Phi_1 V$, into the weak Steklov equation
\eqref{eq:steklov-weak} at level $\nu_k$; multiplicities match by linearity.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:XiisG1}
With $L=A_{m}+W$ as above, $\Xi=\Phi_2/\Phi_1$ is a Steklov eigenfunction of $\Lambda_a$ at
$\nu_1=\lambda_2-\lambda_1=\mu$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Xienergy}
\mathfrak{a}[\Xi]=\mu\,\left\|\phi_1\Xi_0\right\|_2^2=\mu\,\left\|\phi_2\right\|_2^2<\infty,
\qquad \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\rho\,\Xi_0=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\phi_1\phi_2=0 .
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:spectral-corr} with $k=1$: $\phi_2$ maps to a Steklov
eigenfunction at $\nu_1=\mu$, namely $V=\Xi$. The energy identity is
\eqref{eq:corr-quad} with $u=\phi_2$. Orthogonality is
$\int\phi_1^2(\phi_2/\phi_1)=\int\phi_1\phi_2=0$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Corollary~\ref{cor:XiisG1} reduces the oscillation theorem to: the first nonzero Steklov
eigenfunction $g_1$ changes sign exactly once on $(0,\infty)$, since $\phi_2=\phi_1\Xi_0$
and $\phi_1>0$. The correspondence \eqref{eq:corr} also guarantees $\mu=\nu_1$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:osc}
The second radial eigenfunction $\phi_2$ of $L$ changes sign exactly once on
$(0,\infty)$: there is a unique $r_0\in(0,\infty)$ such that, after a choice of sign,
$\phi_2(r)>0$ for $0<r<r_0$ and $\phi_2(r)<0$ for $r>r_0$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:axis}
$\Xi=\Phi_2/\Phi_1$, and more generally any ratio $V=\mathcal{U} u/\Phi_1$ with $u\inH^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}$
smooth, extends to a $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times(0,\infty)$ including the axis
$\{x=0\}$, with $\nabla_x V(0,y)=0$. Consequently $\{r=0\}$ is not an absorbing boundary
for nodal lines.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
$\Phi_j(x,y)=(P^m_y*\phi_j)(x)$ is smooth and, for $\Phi_1$, strictly positive at $x=0$
(Prop.~\ref{prop:phi1pos}); the quotient is $C^\infty$ across the axis. Being $x$-radial
and smooth forces $\nabla_x V(0,y)=0$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:limits}
There is $\xi_\infty\in\mathbb{R}$ with $\Xi(x,y)\to\xi_\infty$ as $\varrho\to\infty$
(exponentially). The trace $\Xi_0(r)=\phi_2(r)/\phi_1(r)$ satisfies
$\Xi_0(0^+),\ \Xi_0(\infty)=\xi_\infty$ finite; the set of sign changes
$\{r_1<\cdots<r_N\}$ is contained in a compact subset of $(0,\infty)$ and $N<\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:ext-reg}, $\Phi_j\sim e^{-m\varrho}\varrho^{-d/2}\psi_j(\theta)$,
$\theta=\arctan(y/r)$, with $\psi_1>0$; hence $\Xi\to\psi_2/\psi_1$. Finite energy
$\mathfrak{a}[\Xi]<\infty$ (Cor.~\ref{cor:XiisG1}) forces $\nabla\Xi\to0$ in the exterior, and
unique continuation (Prop.~\ref{prop:ucp}) forces a single limit $\xi_\infty$. At $y=0$:
$\phi_1(0)>0$, $\phi_2(0)$ finite give $\Xi_0(0^+)$ finite; both $\phi_j$ decay at the
common rate, so $\Xi_0(\infty)=\xi_\infty$ finite. Accumulation of sign changes at $0$ or
$\infty$ would contradict the endpoint limits; each sign change is transversal
(Prop.~\ref{prop:strict}), hence isolated, so $N<\infty$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:poly}
$\left|\Xi(x,y)\right|\le C(1+\varrho)^{C'}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
From the exponential upper bound on $\Phi_2$ (Prop.~\ref{prop:ext-reg}(iii)) and the
exponential lower bound on $\Phi_1$ (Prop.~\ref{prop:ext-reg}(iv)),
$\left|\Xi\right|\le Ce^{-m'\varrho}/(ce^{-m\varrho}\varrho^{-d/2})\le C''\varrho^{d/2}
e^{(m-m')\varrho}$; taking $m'\uparrow m$ gives polynomial growth.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:smp}
Let $\mathcal A V:=\operatorname{div}(a\nabla V)$ with $a=\Phi_1^2\in W^{1,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}$,
$a\ge a_0>0$ on compact subsets. If $\mathcal AV=0$ and $V\ge0$ on an open connected
$\Omega$ with $V(p_0)=0$ at an interior point, then $V\equiv0$ on $\Omega$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Divergence-form strong maximum principle, Gilbarg--Trudinger \cite[Thm.~8.19]{GT}. The
axis $\{r=0\}$ is interior by Lemma~\ref{lem:axis}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:hopf}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:smp}, if $V\ge0$, $V\not\equiv0$,
$V(q_0)=0$ at $q_0\in\{y=0\}$ satisfying an interior ball condition, then
$-\partial_y V(q_0)>0$.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Divergence-form Hopf lemma, Gilbarg--Trudinger \cite[Lem.~3.4]{GT}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:ucp}
Let $a=\Phi_1^2\in C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$. If $\mathcal AV=\operatorname{div}(a\nabla V)=0$ and $V$
vanishes to infinite order at one point of an open connected set $O$, then $V\equiv0$
on $O$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The principal part $a\,\mathrm{Id}$ is Lipschitz ($\Phi_1\in C^\infty$; near the axis, in
Cartesian coordinates, $\partial_{x_i}(\Phi_1^2)=2\Phi_1\partial_{x_i}\Phi_1\in
C^{0,1}_{\rm loc}$), and the operator is uniformly elliptic on compact subsets (the
degeneration $a\to0$ occurs only as $\varrho\to\infty$). Aronszajn's theorem applies
\cite{Aronszajn}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:trunc}
Let $D\subset\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}$ be a nodal domain of a $\nu_1$-eigenfunction $V$. Then
$\Theta_D:=V\mathbf 1_D\in\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{rad}$ with $\nabla\Theta_D=(\nabla V)\mathbf 1_D$ a.e., and
for two distinct nodal domains $D\ne D'$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:no-cross}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}}a\,\nabla\Theta_D\cdot\nabla\Theta_{D'}=0,\qquad
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\rho\,\Theta_{D,0}\,\Theta_{D',0}=0 .
\end{equation}
Moreover $\Theta_D$ solves the Steklov equation on $D$.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:smp}, $V\in C^1$ up to $\partial D\cap\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}$ where $V=0$, so
truncation produces no interface measure and $\Theta_D\in\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{rad}$. The energies $\mathfrak{a}$
and $\left\|\cdot\right\|_\rho^2$ are local integrals;
$\operatorname{supp}\Theta_D\cap\operatorname{supp}\Theta_{D'}\subset\{V=0\}$ has zero measure, giving
\eqref{eq:no-cross}. Testing \eqref{eq:steklov-weak} with $\varphi\mathbf1_D$ (interior
boundary carries $V=0$, no flux) gives the equation on $D$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:crux}
Property \eqref{eq:no-cross} is the decisive difference from $A_{m}$ acting directly. For a
nonlocal form $\iint(u(x)-u(y))^2 J_m(\left|x-y\right|)$, disjoint supports still interact
through the long-range kernel $J_m$, producing cross terms that prevent additivity. The
ratio reduction of Section~\ref{sec:ratio} replaces $A_{m}$ by the local operator
$\operatorname{div}(a\nabla\cdot)$, for which disjoint supports are decoupled.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:cauchy}
Let $V$ solve $\operatorname{div}(a\nabla V)=0$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}$ with $V_0\equiv0$ and
$a\,\partial_y V|_{y=0}\equiv0$ on an open interval $\{r\in(\alpha,\beta),\ y=0\}$. Then
$V\equiv0$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Even reflection $\widetilde V(r,y):=V(r,\left|y\right|)$, reflected weight
$\widetilde a(r,y)=\Phi_1(r,\left|y\right|)^2\in C^{0,1}$ across $y=0$. Vanishing Cauchy data make
$\widetilde V$ vanish to infinite order on $(\alpha,\beta)\times(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$; Aronszajn
UCP (Prop.~\ref{prop:ucp}) gives $\widetilde V\equiv0$ there, and connectedness
propagates $V\equiv0$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:signadd}
Let $V\in\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{rad}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:steklov-weak} at level $\nu_1$, $V^{\pm}=\max(\pm V,0)$.
Then $\mathfrak{a}[V]=\mathfrak{a}[V^+]+\mathfrak{a}[V^-]$,
$\left\|V_0\right\|_\rho^2=\left\|V_0^+\right\|_\rho^2+\left\|V_0^-\right\|_\rho^2$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:signadd2}
\mathfrak{a}[V^{\pm}]=\nu_1\left\|V_0^{\pm}\right\|_\rho^2 .
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
$\nabla V^+\cdot\nabla V^-=0$ a.e.\ and $V_0^+V_0^-=0$ give the additivity. Testing
\eqref{eq:steklov-weak} with $V^+$ ($\nabla V\cdot\nabla V^+=\left|\nabla V^+\right|^2$,
$g V_0^+=V_0^{+2}$) gives
$\mathfrak{a}[V^+]=\nu_1\left\|V_0^+\right\|_\rho^2$; similarly $V^-$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:compadd}
Let $\{V>0\}=\bigsqcup_i\mathcal O_i$ and $W_i:=V\mathbf 1_{\mathcal O_i}$. Then each
$W_i\in\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{rad}$, and for scalars $\gamma_i$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compadd}
\mathfrak{a}\Big[\sum_i\gamma_iW_i\Big]=\sum_i\gamma_i^2\,\mathfrak{a}[W_i],\qquad
\Big\|\sum_i\gamma_iW_{i,0}\Big\|_\rho^2=\sum_i\gamma_i^2\left\|W_{i,0}\right\|_\rho^2,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compadd2}
\mathfrak{a}[W_i]=\nu_1\left\|W_{i,0}\right\|_\rho^2 .
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Disjoint supports and locality give \eqref{eq:compadd} as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:trunc}. Each $W_i$ solves the Steklov equation on $\mathcal O_i$
with $V=0$ on the interior boundary, giving \eqref{eq:compadd2}.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:count}
Let $V\in\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{rad}$ be a $\nu_1$-eigenfunction. Then $V_0$ changes sign exactly once on
$(0,\infty)$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Since $V_0\perp_\rho g_0\equiv\mathrm{const}$, $V_0$ changes sign at least once. Suppose
it changes sign at least twice. Then $\{V>0\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d+1}_{+}$ has at least two connected
components $\mathcal O_1,\mathcal O_2$ meeting $\{y=0\}$ in disjoint intervals. Put
$W_1=V\mathbf 1_{\mathcal O_1}$, $W_2=V\mathbf 1_{\mathcal O_2}$, $W_3=V^-$,
$\mathcal E=\mathrm{span}\{W_1,W_2,W_3\}$, $\dim\mathcal E=3$. By
Lemmas~\ref{lem:signadd}--\ref{lem:compadd}, for $U=\sum_i\gamma_iW_i$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:E-const}
\mathfrak{a}[U]=\sum_i\gamma_i^2\mathfrak{a}[W_i]
=\nu_1\sum_i\gamma_i^2\left\|W_{i,0}\right\|_\rho^2=\nu_1\left\|U_0\right\|_\rho^2,
\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \mathcal R\big|_{\mathcal E}\equiv\nu_1 .
\end{equation}
Choose $0\ne U\in\mathcal E$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-cond}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\rho\,U_0=0,\qquad \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\rho\,U_0\,V_0=0
\end{equation}
(three dimensions, two constraints). Then $\{V_0,U_0\}$ are $\rho$-orthogonal, both
$\perp_\rho g_0$, and $\mathcal R\equiv\nu_1$ on $\mathrm{span}\{V,U\}$; the min--max
principle gives
$\nu_2\le\max_{0\ne\Theta\in\mathrm{span}\{1,V,U\}}\mathcal R[\Theta]=\nu_1$, hence
$\nu_1=\nu_2$ and $U$ is a $\nu_1$-eigenfunction. The trace $U_0$ vanishes on an open
interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$ (since $U$ is supported in a proper subset while $V$ has
full support by Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy}); as a $\nu_1$-eigenfunction,
$a\partial_yU|_0=-\nu_1\rho U_0=0$ on $I$, so both Cauchy data vanish on $I$;
Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy} forces $U\equiv0$, a contradiction. Hence $V_0$ changes sign
exactly once.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:Xi-once}
$\Xi_0=\phi_2/\phi_1$ changes sign exactly once on $(0,\infty)$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
$\Xi$ is a $\nu_1$-eigenfunction (Cor.~\ref{cor:XiisG1}); apply Theorem~\ref{thm:count}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:strict}
At its zero $r_0$, $\Xi_0$ changes sign strictly.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
If $\Xi_0\ge0$ on a one-sided neighbourhood of $r_0$ with $\Xi_0(r_0)=0$, then $(r_0,0)$
is a boundary zero minimum of $\Xi\ge0$, and Hopf (Prop.~\ref{prop:hopf}) gives
$-\Phi_1^2\partial_y\Xi(r_0,0)>0$; but \eqref{eq:Xieq} gives
$-\Phi_1^2\partial_y\Xi(r_0,0)=\mu\phi_1(r_0)^2\Xi_0(r_0)=0$ with $\Phi_1(r_0,0)^2>0$, a
contradiction.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Corollary~\ref{cor:Xi-once} gives one sign change of $\Xi_0$ at $r_0$;
Proposition~\ref{prop:strict} makes it strict; $\phi_1>0$
(Prop.~\ref{prop:phi1pos}). Since $\phi_2=\phi_1\Xi_0$, $\phi_2>0$ on $(0,r_0)$ and
$\phi_2<0$ on $(r_0,\infty)$, with $r_0$ unique.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The proof used only: the extension energy identity (Prop.~\ref{prop:key-IBP}), absorbing
$m^2$ and $W$ into $\Phi_1^2$; the min--max \eqref{eq:minmax}; the strict additivity
\eqref{eq:compadd}--\eqref{eq:compadd2}; and unique continuation
(Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy}). No nodal-set topology, blow-up classification, or monotonicity
of $W$ beyond boundedness were used, so the proof is uniform in $m\in[0,m_*]$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:nondeg}
$\operatorname{ker}L_{+}\capL^{2}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})=\{0\}$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:LplusQ}
$L_{+} Q=-(p-2)Q^{p-1}$; consequently $\left\langle \varphi,Q^{p-1}\right\rangle=0$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
$L_{+} Q=A_{m} Q+Q-(p-1)Q^{p-1}=Q^{p-1}-(p-1)Q^{p-1}=-(p-2)Q^{p-1}$ by \eqref{eq:Qeq}.
Self-adjointness gives
$0=\left\langle L_{+}\varphi,Q\right\rangle=\left\langle \varphi,L_{+} Q\right\rangle=-(p-2)\left\langle \varphi,Q^{p-1}\right\rangle$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:comm}
On $H^{1/2}$, with $\mathcal E:=x\cdot\nabla$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:comm}
[A_{m},\mathcal E]=A_{m}\mathcal E-\mathcal EA_{m}=-A_{m}+m^2A_{m}^{-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
In Fourier variables $\widehat{\mathcal E u}=-(d+\xi\cdot\nabla_\xi)\hat u$ and $A_{m}$ has
symbol $g(\xi)=\sqrt{\left|\xi\right|^2+m^2}$. The commutator of the multiplier $g$ with
$-(d+\xi\cdot\nabla_\xi)$ is multiplication by $\xi\cdot\nabla_\xi g$. Now
$\xi\cdot\nabla_\xi g=\left|\xi\right|^2/g=(g^2-m^2)/g=g-m^2/g$, whose operator is
$A_{m}-m^2A_{m}^{-1}$; the sign convention $\mathcal E=x\cdot\nabla$ (Fourier conjugate
$-(d+\xi\cdot\nabla_\xi)$) gives $[A_{m},\mathcal E]=-(A_{m}-m^2A_{m}^{-1})$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:scaling}
Let $\Lambda Q:=\tfrac1{p-2}Q+x\cdot\nabla Q$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:LplusLambda}
L_{+}(\Lambda Q)=-2Q^{p-1}+Q+m^2A_{m}^{-1}Q .
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Apply $\Lambda$ to \eqref{eq:Qeq}.

\emph{Term $\Lambda(A_{m} Q)$.} With Lemma~\ref{lem:comm}, $\mathcal EA_{m} Q=A_{m}\mathcal E Q
+A_{m} Q-m^2A_{m}^{-1}Q$, and $\mathcal E Q=\Lambda Q-\tfrac1{p-2}Q$, so
\[
\Lambda(A_{m} Q)=\tfrac1{p-2}A_{m} Q+\mathcal EA_{m} Q
=A_{m}\Lambda Q+A_{m} Q-m^2A_{m}^{-1}Q .
\]

\emph{Term $\Lambda(Q^{p-1})$.}
$\Lambda(Q^{p-1})=\tfrac1{p-2}Q^{p-1}+(p-1)Q^{p-2}\mathcal E Q
=(p-1)Q^{p-2}\Lambda Q+\big(\tfrac{1-(p-1)}{p-2}\big)Q^{p-1}
=(p-1)Q^{p-2}\Lambda Q-Q^{p-1}$.

Applying $\Lambda$ to $A_{m} Q+Q=Q^{p-1}$:
\[
A_{m}\Lambda Q+A_{m} Q-m^2A_{m}^{-1}Q+\Lambda Q=(p-1)Q^{p-2}\Lambda Q-Q^{p-1},
\]
i.e.\ $L_{+}\Lambda Q=-A_{m} Q+m^2A_{m}^{-1}Q-Q^{p-1}$. Substituting $A_{m} Q=Q^{p-1}-Q$,
$L_{+}\Lambda Q=-(Q^{p-1}-Q)+m^2A_{m}^{-1}Q-Q^{p-1}=-2Q^{p-1}+Q+m^2A_{m}^{-1}Q$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:polluted}
$\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\varphi\,\big(Q+m^2A_{m}^{-1}Q\big)=0.$
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
$0=\left\langle L_{+}\Lambda Q,\varphi\right\rangle=\left\langle \Lambda Q,L_{+}\varphi\right\rangle=0$, so pairing
\eqref{eq:LplusLambda} with $\varphi$ and using Lemma~\ref{lem:LplusQ} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{prop:dmQ}
Fix $m_0>0$ and $Q_{m_0}\in\mathcal G_{m_0}$ satisfying the tangent
positive-definiteness \eqref{eq:posdef}. Then there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a $C^1$ map
$m\mapsto Q_m\inH^{1/2}_{\mathrm{rad}}$, $Q_m\in\mathcal G_m$, $Q_m|_{m=m_0}=Q_{m_0}$, with
$\partial_m Q_m\inL^{2}_{\mathrm{rad}}$ exponentially decaying, solving weakly
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dmQeq}
L_{+}\,(\partial_m Q_m)=-\,m\,A_{m}^{-1}Q_m .
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
This is Theorem~\ref{thm:cift}, whose only hypothesis is \eqref{eq:posdef}. The identity
\eqref{eq:dmQeq} follows by differentiating $F(m,Q_m)=0$ in $m$, using
